reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: Caused by mosaic tetrasomy of the short arm of chromosome 12, usually from a supernumerary isochromosome 12p present in only a proportion of cells
A characteristic pattern of pigmentary skin anomalies (streaks of hyper- and hypopigmentation) and localised areas of alopecia, along with a coarse face, may develop over time
Facial features include a high forehead with frontotemporal balding, sparse eyebrows and eyelashes, hypertelorism, a short nose with anteverted nares and a long philtrum
Profound hypotonia, severe intellectual disability and epilepsy are typical
Diaphragmatic hernia, congenital heart disease and other malformations are recognised associations
Because the isochromosome is often absent from blood lymphocytes with age, skin fibroblast analysis or buccal sampling is the preferred diagnostic tissue
Recurrence risk is generally low as the abnormality is sporadic and mosaic
reference.pathophysiology: Pallister-Killian syndrome results from mosaic tetrasomy 12p, most often due to a supernumerary isochromosome composed of two copies of the short arm of chromosome 12, giving four copies of 12p in affected cells. The extra genetic material causes an imbalance of dosage-sensitive genes during development. Because the isochromosome is unstable and tends to be lost from rapidly dividing tissues such as blood, the mosaicism is often confined to fibroblasts and other tissues, which accounts for the diagnostic difficulty and the tissue-dependent detection.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia of other genetic cause
additionalInvestigations: Chromosomal analysis or microarray on skin fibroblasts or buccal cells rather than blood, to detect the mosaic isochromosome
FISH for 12p to confirm tetrasomy and estimate the mosaic fraction
Prenatal detection via amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling when suspected antenatally
Imaging to detect diaphragmatic hernia and other structural anomalies
redFlags: Respiratory distress at birth from congenital diaphragmatic hernia
Undiagnosed congenital heart disease causing cardiorespiratory compromise
Severe feeding difficulty with aspiration and failure to thrive
reference.prognosis: Outcome is variable and correlates with the tissue distribution of the mosaicism; many affected children have profound intellectual disability and significant medical needs, and severe cases with diaphragmatic hernia have high early mortality. Those surviving infancy generally live into childhood or beyond with major disability.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis on a normal blood karyotype because the isochromosome is lost from lymphocytes
Failing to test fibroblasts or buccal cells, the tissues most likely to reveal the mosaic
Attributing the pigmentary changes to an unrelated skin disorder
Underestimating the risk of associated diaphragmatic hernia and cardiac anomalies
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Neonatal surgical repair of congenital diaphragmatic hernia and other structural anomalies, with respiratory support
Anti-seizure medication for epilepsy guided by EEG
Management of profound hypotonia and feeding difficulty with physiotherapy, feeding support and gastrostomy where needed
Cardiology review and treatment of congenital heart disease
Developmental support, communication aids and specialist education for severe intellectual disability
Ophthalmology, audiology and dermatology surveillance for associated anomalies
Genetic counselling with confirmatory testing on skin fibroblasts or buccal cells, as the mosaic isochromosome is often absent from blood
Multidisciplinary coordination and family support given the significant medical needs
